fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "The Playing Cards as a Lost Book of Life", "body": "Alexander Dunlop traces his work to a spiritual awakening at 17 and a roughly 20 year search that ran through human design and the Gene Keys before it landed him on the ordinary 52 card deck. He argues the deck is the Book of Life the Bible references, hidden in plain sight, and that in ancient times, before books had bindings, it would have been known in esoteric circles as a little book of our life on Earth. He describes testing it on strangers in New York bars after his divorce, and says he only understood himself once he learned he was born to play the nine of hearts."}, {"title": "Reading the Deck as a Visual Language", "body": "Dunlop's central claim is that the pip layouts are a readable visual language rather than meanings to be memorized, closer to a Chinese character or a hieroglyph. Restored from the standard two and a half by three and a half inch card to what he calls sacred geometric proportions, he says the 12, the so called queen, becomes a golden rectangle, and the 11, the jack, becomes a cube inside a walled garden, Metatron's Cube. Clubs stand for mind, hearts for emotion, diamonds for the physical, spades for consciousness and imagination, the acorn he links to the pineal gland. Every pattern, he says, carries a shadow side."}, {"title": "Two Spreads, Life Paths and the Astrology Overlap", "body": "Laid out in a seven by seven grid with three cards left over, Dunlop works from two charts: the perfect layout he calls the spiritual spread, and the dealt layout he calls the earthly spread, produced by a mathematical deal rather than a shuffle. A birth card comes from the date, while the second card, the planetary ruling card, comes from whichever planet rules your astrological sign, which is why some people get the same card twice. Life paths are read right to left, as in Hebrew. Chance Garton's ace of diamonds and three of clubs, with the Queen of Spades in Pluto, serve as the worked example."}, {"title": "The Calendar Encoded in the Deck", "body": "The correspondence Dunlop says makes it click for most people is calendrical: 52 cards and 52 weeks, four suits and four seasons, 13 cards per suit and 13 weeks per season. Adding the face values, ace as one up to king as 13, gives 364, and he assigns the Joker a value of five quarters to reach 365 and a quarter, with the second Joker as both zero point and leftover. He gives the algorithm for a day's card as 55 minus twice the month plus the day. Asked why a Gregorian calendar should work, he offers only a story of reading for a woman in China through a translator."}, {"title": "Shadow Patterns, Healing Stories and Life as a Game", "body": "The final stretch shifts to health. Dunlop recounts coming home from six months in India and the Osho center at his Saturn return with psoriasis, eczema and severe gut symptoms, being told a doctor could only mitigate them, then spending years on juice cleanses and a gluten free diet before going back to nutrition school. Garton describes leaving allergy injections behind after essential oils, veganism and cutting dairy. Dunlop says clients have lost chronic headaches on seeing their pattern, citing a woman born to play the two of diamonds who used migraines to say no. He offers baseball as the model: a nudge, a slap, then out."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Alexander Dunlop is the author of Play Your Cards Right: A Sacred Guide to Life On Earth. Through his website at The Source Cards, Alexander is a divinatory guide helping people find their place in the fractal blueprint of reality. Does the ubiquitous 52 card deck contain mystical information akin to one's astrological chart? Tune in and find out!
